newsitem.title: USA: U.N. weakness encourages Iraq, Ekeus says.
newsitem.headline: U.N. weakness encourages Iraq, Ekeus says.

text.p: Weakly worded statements by the U.N. Security Council have encouraged Iraq to obstruct efforts by a U.N. commission to scrap its weapons of mass destruction, the head of the commission said on Wednesday.

Rolf Ekeus, chairman of the Special Commission for the Disarmament of Iraq (UNSCOM), told a Washington think-tank that Iraq had become even less cooperative following a Dec. 30 reprimand from the Security Council.
The Council censured Baghdad for refusing to allow more than 100 missile engines to be taken abroad for examination by experts.
"They said...they reminded Iraq about its obligations. It's like I had forgotten to pay my dentist's bill," Ekeus told the Washington Institute for Near East Policy.

"Quite clearly Iraq took the message and...we have met serious obstructions on quite harmless things," he said. "The Iraqis say: 'Well, you see the Council is not backing you...and we therefore see no reason why we should cooperate with you'."

UNSCOM was set up after Iraq's defeat in the 1991 Gulf War but despite six years of inspections and destruction programmes says it believes Iraq is still concealing ballistic missiles and chemical and biological warfare capabilities.
Ekeus said he was briefing Security Council members on the situation and hoped for a "clear and coherent statement of policy" in coming weeks.
But he said he detected in the Security Council "an overall complacency in the sense that fundamentally the situation in Iraq is under control".

Last month an "oil-for-food" deal went into effect permitting Iraq to sell $2 billion worth of oil over six months to buy food and medicines to help offset the effects of U.N. sanctions on Iraqi civilians.

But for Baghdad to obtain full sanctions relief and resume unrestricted oil exports worth an estimated $30 billion a year, UNSCOM must report that Iraq has scrapped its nuclear, chemical, biological and ballistic missile potential.

Ekeus said that Iraq appeared to have adopted a policy of trying "to keep the weapons and get the oil", and was hoping for splits in the Security Council this year as a result of "political fatigue and political attrition."
"What we need is continuing support, political backup, so that there is a will and stomach to keep us there," he said.
Security Council permanent members Russia and France are owed billions of dollars by Iraq for pre-Gulf War weapons sales, which will not be paid back while sanctions continue.
